127.subtitle: Two wombs, then the knowledge that has no edges

commentary.meaning: Eight names in two lines that answer each other. The first line begins with two wombs and ends with speech: she carries the universe inside her, she carries the golden seed from which it comes, she gives to whoever stands lowest, and every utterance made anywhere falls under her authority. The second line turns inward and takes away about as much as it grants. She is arrived at by meditation and by no other road; she cannot be cut around or measured off; she hands over knowledge; and she is knowledge with a body. The hinge between the halves is what makes the verse a verse rather than a list. The first four names sketch a goddess who contains everything and gives freely, which is the vocabulary of cosmology and of petition. The last four describe something no petition reaches and no definition encloses, and that can be had only as a gift. Between avaradā, who gives to the least, and jñānadā, who gives knowledge, the verse has quietly changed what is worth asking for.
commentary.history:
The two wombs at the head of the verse are not a repetition. Garbha in Sanskrit covers the womb, the embryo, and the interior of anything, and the two compounds are bahuvrīhis that use it in slightly different senses. Viśvagarbhā says that the whole world is inside her, which makes her the container. Svarṇagarbhā says that the gold is inside her, which makes her the mother of a container. The gold in question is the hiraṇyagarbha, the golden germ of Ṛgveda 10.121, one of the oldest cosmogonic images in Indian literature: a single embryo of gold that arises at the beginning, becomes the one lord of everything born, and holds heaven and earth in place. Later systems fix hiraṇyagarbha as a technical term for the first differentiated stage of the cosmos, the totality of subtle bodies, the collective mind before there are individual minds — the level that Brahmā personifies. To call her svarṇagarbhā is therefore to place her one step behind the oldest thing the tradition can name. Hiraṇyagarbha is the first-born; she is what he is born from.

The third name is the one to slow down at, and the printed line here is worth reading carefully. The text gives svarṇagarbhā'varadā, and the avagraha — the mark ऽ that stands for a swallowed short a — tells you that the name underneath the sandhi is avaradā, not varadā. Long ā plus short a produces long ā and leaves the mark behind as a receipt. This matters because varadā, giver of boons, is one of the commonest epithets in the entire literature, and a reciter working by ear alone will hear it here and be wrong. The commentators offer two ways of taking avaradā, and both are current. Read avara as low, inferior, hindmost, and the name means she who gives to the lowest, so that no petitioner is too far down the scale to be reached. Read the a- as the negative prefix attached to varadā and the name means she who is not a mere giver of boons, on the grounds that a boon is a small thing to want from her and that what she actually gives is named five syllables later as knowledge. The second reading is the more startling and fits the movement of the verse; the first is the more natural Sanskrit. Nothing requires choosing, and the tradition has generally been content to let the ambiguity stand.

Vāgadhīśvarī, overlord of speech, joins this hymn to the Vedic figure of Vāc, who in Ṛgveda 10.125 speaks in the first person and claims to move with all the gods, to bend the bow of Rudra, and to make whomever she loves into a sage. Śrīvidyā inherits that identification wholesale: speech is not something the goddess governs from outside but something she is, articulated through the levels that the tradition calls parā, paśyantī, madhyamā and vaikharī — speech at rest, speech seen, speech in the middle, speech that comes out of a mouth. The doubled superlative in the name is deliberate. Adhi means over and above; īśvarī is already a sovereign lady; adhīśvarī is the sovereign over sovereigns. Sarasvatī is the goddess of speech, and this name says who stands over her.

The second line moves into the vocabulary of Vedānta. Aparicchedyā is built on pariccheda, cutting around, which in that literature is the standard word for limitation, and the standard analysis names three kinds: limitation by place, by time, and by thing — deśa, kāla and vastu. A pot is here and not there, now and not then, a pot and not a cloth. The name denies all three of her at once, and it does so with a gerundive, aparicchedyā, not able to be delimited: the point is not that no one has yet drawn the line but that the line cannot be drawn. Set beside dhyānagamyā, to be approached by meditation, it produces the characteristic double motion of these hymns. She is unreachable by definition and reachable by absorption, and the two claims are not in tension because dhyāna is precisely the operation that stops producing definitions.

The verse closes by distinguishing the gift from the giver. Jñānadā makes knowledge something handed over rather than achieved, which is the position the Upaniṣads take when they say that the self is not obtained by exposition or by intelligence or by much hearing, but by the one whom it chooses. Jñānavigrahā then removes the last distance: vigraha is body, bodily form, the word used for the image in a temple, and the compound says that in her case the knowledge and the body are the same substance. What would be flesh in anyone else is, in her, knowing.
commentary.practice:
This verse contains the first serious tongue-twister of its neighbourhood, and it is the sandhi rather than the sound that catches people. The second and third names run together as svarṇagarbhā'varadā, a single unbroken stretch of seven syllables, and the reciter has to know that a name boundary falls inside it. Say svarṇagarbhā, then varadā, with no pause and no fresh breath but with the knowledge that you have just said two names. When the same verse is chanted as an archanā, name by name with namaḥ after each, the sandhi is undone and the hidden a comes back: svarṇagarbhāyai namaḥ, avaradāyai namaḥ. Hearing the a return is the best proof that it was there.

The conjunct ज्ञ in jñānadā and jñānavigrahā is pronounced in at least three different ways across India, and reciters are often surprised to learn this. Its analysed value is a palatal j followed by the palatal nasal ñ, which is what the transliteration jñā records and what most southern traditions approximate. Much of the north says gya, so that jñāna comes out as gyāna; Marathi speakers say dnya. None of these will get you thrown out of a recitation hall. What matters more for the metre is that the following ā is long in both names and that the two names are not identical: jñānadā has three syllables, jñānavigrahā has five, and the second one carries the weight of the pāda.

Aparicchedyā is the hardest single word here. It contains cch, which is not a long ch but an unaspirated palatal stop followed by an aspirated one — c then ch, two separate articulations, the second with a puff of breath. English has nothing that behaves this way, and the usual failure is to produce a single soft ch and lose a full beat of the line. Then comes dyā, dental d plus the palatal glide, again with no vowel between. Practise the word in three pieces at half speed, a-pari-cchedyā, and only then put it back together.

The metre is standard anuṣṭubh, eight syllables to the quarter, and the break falls after the sixteenth syllable, which here is the end of aparicchedyā. That places the caesura exactly where the sense breaks too: everything before it is about extent, everything after it is about knowing. Breathe there and nowhere else in the verse.

For the recitation done as offering, note that six of these eight names are feminine ā-stems and take the dative in -āyai — viśvagarbhāyai, svarṇagarbhāyai, avaradāyai, dhyānagamyāyai, aparicchedyāyai, jñānadāyai, jñānavigrahāyai — while vāgadhīśvarī, being an ī-stem, becomes vāgadhīśvaryai. That single irregularity in the middle of the verse is a useful place to notice that the endings are grammar and not decoration.

As for what to hold while saying it: the verse gives two wombs, a gift to the lowest, and the mastery of every word, and then says that none of it can be delimited and that the knowledge of it has to be given. It is a good verse for someone who has been working hard at study, and it is not flattering to that effort.

crossReferences.deva: हिरण्यगर्भः समवर्तताग्रे भूतस्य जातः पतिरेक आसीत् । स दाधार पृथिवीं द्यामुतेमां कस्मै देवाय हविषा विधेम ॥
crossReferences.iast: hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre bhūtasya jātaḥ patir eka āsīt | sa dādhāra pṛthivīṃ dyām utemāṃ kasmai devāya haviṣā vidhema ||
crossReferences.translation: In the beginning the golden germ came into being; once born, he was the one lord of all that exists. He held this earth in place, and the sky as well. To which god shall we offer our oblation?
crossReferences.relevance: The source of svarṇagarbhā. The hymn's golden embryo is the first thing there is, the one that holds heaven and earth apart, and every later system treats hiraṇyagarbha as the earliest name for a differentiated cosmos. The sahasranāma takes that figure and makes it the contents of her womb, which is a considerable claim made in four syllables.

crossReferences.source: Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3 (the same verse stands at Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.23)
crossReferences.deva: नायमात्मा प्रवचनेन लभ्यो न मेधया न बहुना श्रुतेन । यमेवैष वृणुते तेन लभ्यस्तस्यैष आत्मा विवृणुते तनूं स्वाम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: nāyam ātmā pravacanena labhyo na medhayā na bahunā śrutena | yam evaiṣa vṛṇute tena labhyas tasyaiṣa ātmā vivṛṇute tanūṃ svām ||
crossReferences.translation: This self is not got by exposition, nor by intelligence, nor by hearing a great deal. It is got by the one whom it chooses; to him this self uncovers its own body.
crossReferences.relevance: The doctrinal warrant for jñānadā, and the reason the name is a giver-compound rather than an epithet of brilliance. Knowledge here is transferred, not earned, and the choosing is done from the other side. The verse even ends with the word tanū, body, which is what jñānavigrahā supplies in the next breath.

crossReferences.source: Ṛgveda 10.125.5 (the Devī Sūkta, spoken by Vāc)
crossReferences.deva: यं कामये तंतमुग्रं कृणोमि तं ब्रह्माणं तमृषिं तं सुमेधाम् ।
crossReferences.iast: yaṃ kāmaye taṃ-tam ugraṃ kṛṇomi taṃ brahmāṇaṃ tam ṛṣiṃ taṃ sumedhām |
crossReferences.translation: Whomever I love, him I make formidable — him a priest, him a seer, him a man of good understanding.
crossReferences.relevance: Vāc speaking for herself, and the oldest statement of what vāgadhīśvarī means. Speech is not a faculty she supervises but a person who distributes intelligence at her own discretion, which places this half-line very close to jñānadā two names later.

references.title: Lalitā Sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library, repeatedly reprinted)
references.note: The one English window onto the eighteenth-century commentary that the tradition treats as authoritative. The translation is Victorian and occasionally opaque, but it is the place to see how much argument sits behind a name like avaradā, where the commentator has to decide whether the a- is a prefix or part of the stem.

references.title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India
references.author: tr. Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton (Oxford University Press, 2014)
references.note: The complete Ṛgveda in three volumes with real introductions to each hymn. Read their headnotes to 10.121 and 10.125 before deciding what svarṇagarbhā and vāgadhīśvarī are borrowing; both hymns are stranger and more argumentative than the devotional tradition usually admits.

references.title: Vāc: The Concept of the Word in Selected Hindu Tantras
references.author: André Padoux, tr. Jacques Gontier (SUNY Press, 1990)
references.note: The standard account of how the tantric traditions understand speech, including the four levels from parā down to the spoken word. Necessary if vāgadhīśvarī is to mean anything more specific than a compliment.

references.title: The Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: V. S. Apte
references.note: Better than Monier-Williams for this verse, because Apte is generous with compounds and gives the range of avara — low, inferior, later, hindmost — that makes both readings of avaradā visible at a glance.

references.title: A Thousand Teachings: The Upadeśasāhasrī of Śaṅkara
references.author: tr. Sengaku Mayeda (SUNY Press, 1992)
references.note: For the second line. Mayeda's introduction lays out the Advaita analysis of limitation by place, time and object that aparicchedyā denies, and does it in plain enough language that a reader without Sanskrit can follow what is being ruled out.
